query: For a FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy used as a thin coating on a conventional metal substrate, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs overall wear resistance and microscopic deformation during sliding in the intended high-temperature operating regime? Define a controlled change relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the corresponding directional changes in wear and deformation, state the regime in which those predictions should hold, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Varying the TiC content in the FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy coating will influence its wear resistance and microscopic deformation during sliding in the high-temperature operating regime.
generation.material_initial_state: FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy coating on a conventional metal substrate
generation.intervention: Varying the TiC content in the alloy
generation.mechanism: Fine-grain strengthening and dispersion strengthening due to the addition of TiC
generation.predicted_outcome: Increased TiC content will enhance the hardness and wear resistance of the coating, leading to decreased wear loss and microscopic deformation during sliding
generation.boundary: High-temperature operating regime, up to a certain TiC content threshold beyond which the benefits of TiC addition may plateau or decrease
generation.uncertainty: Optimal TiC content for maximum wear resistance and minimal deformation, potential interactions between TiC and other alloying elements

falsification_experiment.design: Controlled variable experiment with varying TiC content in the FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy coating
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the wear loss and microscopic deformation do not decrease with increasing TiC content up to a certain threshold, or if the hardness does not increase with TiC addition, the hypothesis is falsified

cited_evidence.text: Zhang et al. [] prepared a composite powder coating of TC4 and WC on the surface of TC4 titanium alloy. The results showed that adding 5%, 10%, and 15% WC content could help improve the microhardness and wear resistance of the coating, and the coating forming quality was good without cracks and other obvious defects. Chong et al. [] added 5% WC into AlCoCrFeNi high entropy alloy powder, and the research showed that WC enhanced the hardness of the AlCoCrFeNi coating, reduced the surface roughness, and improved the wear and corrosion resistance. Hu et al. used high-speed laser cladding to prepare a Ni/WC composite powder coating. The research showed that WC improves the microhardness and wear resistance of the coating and can refine the grain structure, and the decomposition of C and W elements precipitated from the coating played a solid solution strengthening role. Ma et al. [] studied the microstructure, microhardness, and wear resistance of a 60% WC-reinforced FeCoNiCr composite coating prepared by laser cladding. The results showed that the composite coating had good forming quality and better microhardness and wear resistance.

AbstractAl1.8CrCuFeNi2 high-entropy alloy coatings with different TiC contents were prepared using laser cladding. The effect of TiC on the microstructure, hardness and wear resistance of the coatings was investigated. It was found that the phase structure of the coating with 10 wt.% TiC was a single BCC phase with no other precipitated phase. When 20 wt.% TiC was added, the phase structure of the coating was a BCC phase and TiC phase. When the TiC content increased to 30 wt.%, more TiC-reinforcing phase was formed. With the increase in the TiC content, the hardness of the high-entropy alloy coating was enhanced and the wear loss clearly decreased, which was closely related to the change in the coating structure. The addition of TiC to high-entropy alloys plays the role of fine-grain strengthening and dispersion strengthening.Keywords: high-entropy alloys, wear resistance, coatings, titanium carbide

cited_evidence.text: Due to the excellent strength and hardness of 65 Mn high-carbon spring steel, it has become the main material for wear-resistant parts. In this study, 65 Mn spring steel was selected as the matrix material to investigate the wear resistance of the coating. The Al1.8CrCuFeNi2 HEA exhibited high hardness and excellent wear resistance in our previous study []. Therefore, Al1.8CrCuFeNi2 HEA was selected as the main coating material. The 200 mesh Al1.8CrCuFeNi2 HEA powders prefabricated using an aerosol method (Linyi Research and Innovation Material Technology Co., Ltd., Linyi, China.) were used. TiC was selected as the strengthening phase due to its extremely high hardness (above 3000 HV) and low density (4.93 g/cm3). Its excellent microstructure makes it a high-quality nucleation core in the alloy system to promote grain refinement. Moreover, the high hardness and high melting point of TiC particles enable them to be pinned between grains, which plays the role of second-phase strengthening and greatly improves the hardness and wear resistance of the material [].

decision.trend: Research on high-entropy alloys has shown a trend towards investigating their wear resistance and deformation behavior. Earlier studies have focused on the microstructure and properties of these alloys, while more recent studies have explored their potential applications in coatings and nanopillars. The use of laser cladding and other fabrication techniques has been shown to improve the wear resistance and hardness of these alloys.
decision.unsolved: The governing mechanisms of wear resistance and deformation in high-entropy alloys, particularly in the high-temperature operating regime, remain unclear. Further research is needed to understand the relationships between the microstructure, properties, and wear behavior of these alloys.
decision.lever: varying the TiC content in the alloy
decision.why: Based on the trend of researching wear resistance and deformation behavior in high-entropy alloys, the next step would be to investigate the effect of varying the TiC content on the wear resistance and hardness of the alloy. This could involve fabricating coatings with different TiC contents using laser cladding and evaluating their wear behavior and microstructure.
